description:
Earthset is a team from Lahore, Pakistan, taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. At the Moon's south pole the Sun skims barely two degrees above the horizon, so one crater rim can decide whether a mission has power. We're building a fast, intuitive tool to compare landing sites and dates in seconds using NASA's JPL Horizons and LOLA terrain data.

Ibrahim: design, front-end, back-end & APIs
Zafir Ahmed: research, data validation & presentation
summary:
Earthset answers the question every lunar south pole mission depends on: can we land here, and when? For any site and date it checks whether a lander gets sunlight for power and can talk directly to Earth. Near the pole the Sun skims a degree or two above the horizon, so one crater rim can decide both.

Pick one of 28 sites (NASA south pole points, 9 Artemis III regions, CLPS, Apollo and international landers) or click any point on the map. Earthset draws the Sun and Earth against the site's real LOLA terrain skyline in a 360° view, a polar map and walkable 3D terrain. Every hour from 2026 to 2032 gives Sun elevation, sunlit share, Earth visibility, Deep Space Network link windows and countdowns to sunset and Earthset. Set your battery limit and landing Sun range, and each site gets a GO / NO-GO verdict with its next landing window. The Plan page lists every site's next landing date, GO first. Sites can be ranked or compared, and a Learn page explains it for students and the public.

Accuracy first: SPICE positions match JPL Horizons to 0.003 arcseconds, polar sunlight falls inside Barker et al. 2021's published range, and landing windows match a brute-force check 84/84. Everything runs in the browser with no login, so when a launch slips, planners re-check every site in seconds.
details:
What it does

Earthset is a lunar landing site navigator for the Moon's south pole. Choose a site and a date, and it shows where the Sun and Earth sit against that site's real terrain horizon. From that it answers the question a mission depends on: can we land here, and when? It gives a GO / NO-GO verdict built on two things: whether the lander gets sunlight for power, and whether it can talk straight to Earth.

• Site: a mission verdict (GO / NO-GO, next landing window, full light after touchdown, first night against your battery), a 360° skyline view, a polar map and a 3D view of NASA terrain you can walk at lander height. It shows the live Sun and Earth plus countdowns to the next sunset, Earthset and change in the Earth link.

• Plan: enter your battery limit, landing Sun range and earliest landing date, and every site's next landing window appears in one table, GO sites first. One click opens that site at that exact hour.

• Point: click anywhere on the map or type coordinates, and your browser builds that point's skyline from NASA terrain in seconds.

• Rank and Compare: order up to six sites by one measure (sunlight, longest night, Earth in view, landing hours), or put two sites or dates head to head hour by hour. Results export as a PDF report or CSV.

• Learn: a plain-language explainer for students and the public on why a few metres of height matter at the pole.

• Proof: eight accuracy checks, each with its result and the command that re-runs it.

How it works

• Ephemeris: Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/NAIF SPICE (DE440) in the Moon's own body-fixed frame (MOON_ME), so libration is built in, with light-time and stellar-aberration correction.

• Skyline: from each site, rays in 1,440 directions (every 0.25°) out to 300 km across NASA terrain on a curved Moon, using the finest data available: LOLA 5 m maps, then 20 m and 80 m polar maps, SLDEM2015, and LROC NAC terrain models at the Apollo sites.

• Timeline: every hour from 2026 to 2032. The Sun counts as visible while any part of its disk clears the skyline, and Earth while its centre does. There is no air on the Moon, so no refraction correction is needed.

• Link to Earth: a link window also needs a Deep Space Network station (Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra) to see the Moon at least 6° above its horizon, as in NASA's DSN handbook 810-005.

• GO / NO-GO: a landing window needs the Sun up in your landing range and Earth in view for at least 24 hours. The battery must outlast the first night, counted as hours with less than your panel threshold of the Sun's disk visible (default 50%, adjustable in Settings). A grazing sliver of Sun is not daylight for a solar panel.

• Delivery: the heavy work is precomputed in Python and shipped as static files, so the site runs fully in the browser with no server, login or API key.

Benefits and intended impact

Landing dates slip and site lists change. Expert tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons are powerful, but slow for a quick "what if we land two weeks later?" question. Earthset answers it in seconds: a planner sets a battery limit and landing Sun range once, and every page judges every site against them, ending in a clear GO or NO-GO with the next landing date. It also gives educators and the public a true-to-scale picture of why the south pole is so hard: the Sun sits only a degree or two above the horizon, so one ridge decides power and communication.

Accuracy: every number is checked against NASA

• Sun and Earth positions match NASA JPL Horizons to 0.003 arcseconds across 143 positions.

• Sunlight at Connecting ridge (82.6% at 1 m, 88.8% at 5 m) falls inside Barker et al. 2021's published 69.6–86.8% and 88.1–91.1%.

• Our terrain puts IM-1 Odysseus at 2,592 m; NASA's LRO team measured 2,579 m after landing, 13 m apart on a 12° slope.

• The longest sunlit stretch each midsummer agrees within 2 days with Wueller et al. 2026 in 50 of 63 cases, using different software and terrain. Where sites differ we report it instead of tuning the gap away.

• Deep Space Network geometry matches JPL Horizons to 2.3 arcseconds.

• The browser's results match our Python build to 1.8 arcseconds over 28 sites and 490,560 hours. The 3D shadows match the validated skyline in 99.93% of hours.

• Landing windows and GO / NO-GO match a brute-force scan of the Python timelines in 84 of 84 cases.

Tools, languages and software

Python (SpiceyPy, NumPy, Numba, Rasterio) for the data pipeline and checks. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with three.js for the website and 3D terrain, using Web Workers. Hosted on Cloudflare Workers. No special hardware was needed.

What makes it creative

You can stand on real NASA terrain at lander height and watch the true-size Sun disk slide behind a crater rim, with the 3D shadows checked against the same skyline the numbers use. The Sun is drawn at its true angular size, so a half-hidden Sun reads as half power, and the GO / NO-GO verdict uses the same idea. Plan turns months of lighting data into one table of landing dates. Comparisons are a tug of war you can scrub hour by hour. A guided tour, a one-click "Try a 100 h battery" and keyboard shortcuts make it quick to learn.

Factors we considered

• Accuracy and traceability first: each published viewpoint is used as given, never moved by hand, and the LOLA height errors give each skyline point an uncertainty.

• Honesty about limits: the known limits are listed on the Proof page, including the 50% panel threshold, since NASA publishes no single cut-off.

• Accessibility: larger-text and reduced-motion settings, table versions of the main charts, and full keyboard control.

• Speed and cost: static files, with no server to maintain or overload; 3D terrain is prefetched quietly in the background.

• Respect for NASA servers: data is fetched once, cached and requested slowly.
